title: Firewalls
hook: Not every packet that shows up at your server's door is one you actually asked for.

steps.caption: Your normal request reaches the firewall first, before the server ever sees it.

nodeCaptions.firewall: A firewall sits in front of the server and checks every packet against a set of rules before deciding what happens next.

steps.caption: It matches the rules, so the firewall lets it through to the server.

nodeCaptions.server: The server only ever sees traffic the firewall has already approved.

steps.caption: Now someone else sends a packet the rules don't allow.

nodeCaptions.attacker: This packet was addressed to the server, same as any other — the firewall is what stands in its way.
nodeCaptions.firewall: It never reaches the server. The firewall drops it right here, based on its rules.

takeaways: A firewall doesn't block "bad people" — it blocks packets that don't match its rules, whoever sent them.
The server never even knows a blocked packet existed — the firewall stops it before it arrives.
The same firewall that blocks unwanted traffic lets your own legitimate requests straight through.

quiz.question: Where does a firewall stop a blocked packet?
choices: At the server, after it's been processed
At the firewall itself, before it ever reaches the server
It doesn't stop the packet, it just logs it
quiz.explanation: The firewall sits in front of the server and drops disallowed packets there — the server is never involved.

quiz.question: What decides whether the firewall blocks a packet?
choices: Whether the sender has bad intentions
Whether the packet matches the firewall's configured rules
Whether the server is currently busy
quiz.explanation: Firewalls evaluate rules — source/destination, port, protocol — not intent. A misconfigured rule can block legitimate traffic or let malicious traffic through.
